uncited: Standard Fourier Positional Encoding maps low-dimensional input coordinates (typically 3D spatial positions) into a higher-dimensional space using interleaved sine and cosine functions at exponentially increasing frequencies.
It differs from its siblings by using fixed, deterministic frequencies rather than learned or randomized ones, serving as a static feature initialization layer for subsequent neural processing.
- Feature Vector: A concatenated array of sine and cosine evaluations.

Concatenate all components in the order: $[\sin(\gamma_0 \mathbf{x}), \cos(\gamma_0 \mathbf{x}), \sin(\gamma_1 \mathbf{x}), \cos(\gamma_1 \mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(\gamma_{L-1} \mathbf{x}), \cos(\gamma_{L-1} \mathbf{x})]$.
- Degenerate Input: If input coordinates are zero, all sine components are zero and cosine components are one, providing no gradient signal for the sine terms initially.
- Time Complexity: $O(L \cdot D)$, where $L$ is the number of frequencies and $D$ is the input dimension.
- Memory Complexity: $O(L \cdot D)$ to store the output feature vector.
- Limitations: Fixed frequencies may not adapt to specific scene complexities; requires careful frequency range selection to avoid aliasing or underfitting.
- When to use: As a standard initialization for implicit neural fields where high-frequency detail recovery is needed.

- When not to use: When adaptive frequency learning is preferred (see [Fourier Feature Networks](2765-fourier-feature-networks.md)) or when rotational invariance is critical without additional modifications.
Originating from the SIREN framework and popularized by Mildenhall et al. in the context of NeRF, this method uses sinusoidal functions to embed coordinates.
It is commonly used in neural radiance fields and implicit surface representations to enable MLPs to capture fine geometric details.
